# 🔬 Shocks, collapses, synchrony and fleets

📦 **Data**: [FAO Global Capture
Production](https://www.fao.org/fishery/collection/capture/en), release
**2026.1.0** (published by FAO on 2026-03-30; catches 1950–2024),
downloaded from
[Capture_2026.1.0.zip](https://www.fao.org/fishery/static/Data/Capture_2026.1.0.zip).
Licence [CC BY 4.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/).
[`fao_data_info()`](https://linbojun99.github.io/faofishingreport/reference/fao_data_info.md)
shows the release you use and how to cite it.

The five functions of this article follow methods published in the
fisheries and ecology literature. Each section gives the method with its
sources, so that the results can be checked against the original
studies, and says which settings are choices of this package rather than
of those studies. The full references are at the end of the page.

- [`catch_shocks()`](https://linbojun99.github.io/faofishingreport/reference/catch_shocks.md),
  [`collapse_analysis()`](https://linbojun99.github.io/faofishingreport/reference/collapse_analysis.md)
  and
  [`catch_synchrony()`](https://linbojun99.github.io/faofishingreport/reference/catch_synchrony.md)
  take catch data, like the summary analyses: a fishing area from
  [`fishing_area_data()`](https://linbojun99.github.io/faofishingreport/reference/fishing_area_data.md),
  or any subset of
  [`load_fao_data()`](https://linbojun99.github.io/faofishingreport/reference/load_fao_data.md)
  (see [💾 FAO
  data](https://linbojun99.github.io/faofishingreport/articles/data.md)).
- [`distant_water_profile()`](https://linbojun99.github.io/faofishingreport/reference/distant_water_profile.md)
  takes a country and follows its catch in all FAO areas.
- [`compare_releases()`](https://linbojun99.github.io/faofishingreport/reference/compare_releases.md)
  takes two releases of the FAO data.

The examples use the Eastern Central Atlantic (FAO area 34). The charts
are saved in `figures/png/summary/` and the tables in `tables/`. The
pelagic/demersal ratio,
[`pelagic_demersal()`](https://linbojun99.github.io/faofishingreport/reference/pelagic_demersal.md),
belongs to the same group of analyses and is described in [📈
Composition, stock status and
trends](https://linbojun99.github.io/faofishingreport/articles/status-trends.md).

``` r

FAO34 <- fishing_area_data("Atlantic, Eastern Central")
```

The five functions share these arguments:

| Argument | Meaning | Default |
|----|----|----|
| `plot` | Save the charts in `figures/png/summary/` | `TRUE` |
| `table` | Save the tables in `tables/` | `TRUE` |
| `lang` | Language of the charts and names: `"en"`, `"zh"` or `"both"`; `NULL` uses the language set with [`fao_settings()`](https://linbojun99.github.io/faofishingreport/reference/fao_settings.md) | `NULL` |
| `pptx` | Also save the charts as editable PowerPoint files in `figures/pptx/summary/` | `FALSE`, or `TRUE` after `fao_settings(pptx = TRUE)` |
| `label` | Name at the start of the file names | The fishing area (or the country) of the data |

They return their results invisibly: assign them
(`x <- catch_shocks(...)`) to use the tables.

## 📝 In the Word report

[`fao_report()`](https://linbojun99.github.io/faofishingreport/reference/fao_report.md)
can add four of these analyses to the Word report of a fishing area (see
[📝 Assessment report: Word, LaTeX and
PDF](https://linbojun99.github.io/faofishingreport/articles/report.md)).
They are switched off by default:

``` r

fao_report(34, shocks = TRUE, collapse = TRUE, synchrony = TRUE, distant = TRUE)
```

The settings of each function are given with the name of its section as
prefix:

``` r

fao_report(34, shocks = TRUE, collapse = TRUE, synchrony = TRUE, distant = TRUE,
           shocks_method = "gephart2017",   # catch_shocks(method = "gephart2017")
           collapse_method = "worm2006",    # collapse_analysis(method = "worm2006")
           collapse_seed = 2,               # seed of the random series of the null model
           synchrony_by = "country",        # catch_synchrony(by = "country")
           distant_countries = 5,           # profiles of the 5 main distant-water countries
           distant_min_catch = 100)         # distant_water_profile(min_catch = 100)
```

| Section | Function | Settings of the report only |
|----|----|----|
| `shocks` | [`catch_shocks()`](https://linbojun99.github.io/faofishingreport/reference/catch_shocks.md) |  |
| `collapse` | [`collapse_analysis()`](https://linbojun99.github.io/faofishingreport/reference/collapse_analysis.md) | `collapse_seed`: seed of the random series of the null model, default `1`, so that the report gives the same numbers every time |
| `synchrony` | [`catch_synchrony()`](https://linbojun99.github.io/faofishingreport/reference/catch_synchrony.md) |  |
| `distant` | [`distant_water_profile()`](https://linbojun99.github.io/faofishingreport/reference/distant_water_profile.md) | `distant_countries`: the number of countries profiled, default `3` (the countries with the largest distant-water catch in the area over the last five years), or their names, e.g. `c("China", "Japan")` |
| `pelagic` | [`pelagic_demersal()`](https://linbojun99.github.io/faofishingreport/reference/pelagic_demersal.md) |  |

[`compare_releases()`](https://linbojun99.github.io/faofishingreport/reference/compare_releases.md)
compares two versions of the data rather than describing a fishing area,
so it is not a section of the report.

## ⚡ Catch shocks

A shock is a sudden, unusually large fall in production from one year to
the next. Gephart et al. (2017) proposed a statistical method to find
shocks in national fish production series, and Cottrell et al. (2019)
used a version of it to compare shocks in crop, livestock, fisheries and
aquaculture production.
[`catch_shocks()`](https://linbojun99.github.io/faofishingreport/reference/catch_shocks.md)
applies both versions to FAO catch series and counts how often shocks
happen, by year and by group.

### Method

By default a series is the catch of one country in one FAO area
(`by = c("country", "area")`). It runs from its first year with catch to
the last year of the data, with missing years counted as zero. In each
series:

1.  The catch $`c_t`$ is smoothed, and the residuals
    $`r_t = c_t - \hat{c}_t`$ from the smooth are kept.
2.  The residuals are regressed on those of the year before:
    $`r_t = a + b\,r_{t-1} + e_t`$ (a lag-1 regression).
3.  Years whose **Cook’s distance** in this regression is above a
    threshold are candidate shocks. Cook’s distance measures how much
    one observation changes the fitted regression, so it picks out years
    that break the usual year-to-year pattern.
4.  A candidate is kept only if the catch fell below a **baseline**
    $`B_t`$ computed from the preceding years. The loss is $`B_t - c_t`$
    tonnes, or $`100\,(B_t - c_t)/B_t`$ percent.
5.  The shock has recovered in the first later year in which the catch
    is back to at least 95% of $`B_t`$.

The two methods differ in the smoother, the threshold and the baseline:

|  | `"cottrell2019"` (default) | `"gephart2017"` |
|----|----|----|
| Smoother | LOESS, span 0.6 | lowess, span 2/3 |
| Cook’s distance above | 0.3 | 0.35 |
| Baseline $`B_t`$ | Median catch of the previous 7 years | Mean catch of the previous 5 years |
| Earliest possible shock | 8th year of the series | 6th year of the series |
| Source | Cottrell et al. (2019), Methods, and their [code](https://github.com/cottrellr/shocks) | Gephart et al. (2017), section 2, and their [code](https://github.com/jagephart/Shock_Detection) |

Two summaries follow from the shocks:

- the **shock frequency** of a year: the number of shocks divided by the
  number of series with catch in that year, in percent (Cottrell et
  al. 2019);
- the **shock rate** of a group (an area, a country, a continent or a
  species group): the number of shocks divided by the number of series
  in the group (Gephart et al. 2017).

Two settings are choices of this package. Series with catch in fewer
than `min_years` years (20) are left out, because neither study gives a
minimum length. The series of countries that no longer exist (e.g. the
USSR) end in their last year with catch, so that the end of a country is
not counted as a shock.

### Example

``` r

shocks <- catch_shocks(FAO34$area_data)
```

**Reading the results.** In area 34, 48 country series have catch in at
least 20 years, and 22 shocks were found in 20 of them. The shock
frequency is at most 5.6% in any year: shocks are rare events in any one
series. `recovery_years` is the number of years until the catch was back
to 95% of the baseline; `NA` means it had not recovered by the end of
the series (12 of the 22 shocks). The USSR, a former country, and “Other
nei” (catch not attributed to a country) have no continent in the FAO
country list and are shown as `NA`.

### Other settings

The method of Gephart et al. (2017). The file names do not include the
method, so `label` keeps the charts of this call from replacing those of
the first one:

``` r

gephart <- catch_shocks(FAO34$area_data, method = "gephart2017", label = "FAO34 gephart2017")
```

![FAO34_gephart2017_shocks.png](data:image/png;base64,)

`figures/png/summary/FAO34_gephart2017_shocks.png`

``` r

both <- merge(shocks$shocks[, c("series", "Year")], gephart$shocks[, c("series", "Year")])
c(cottrell2019 = nrow(shocks$shocks), gephart2017 = nrow(gephart$shocks), both = nrow(both))
#> cottrell2019  gephart2017         both 
#>           22           26           13
```

The two methods find 22 and 26 shocks, and only 13 of them in the same
series and year: with a threshold close to the Cook’s distance of many
years, the smoother and the baseline decide the borderline cases.
Results that hold with both methods are the more robust.

With `by = "species"`, a series is the catch of one species item in the
area, all countries together, and the shock rate is also given by
ISSCAAP species group:

``` r

species_shocks <- catch_shocks(FAO34$area_data, by = "species", label = "FAO34 species")
```

![FAO34_species_shocks_by_species_group.png](data:image/png;base64,)

`figures/png/summary/FAO34_species_shocks_by_species_group.png`

``` r
groups <- subset(species_shocks$by_group, grouping == "species_group" & n_series >= 5)
show_table(data.frame(groups[, c("group_name", "n_series", "n_shocks", "shocks_per_series")], row.names = NULL))
```

The two studies analysed national totals, all species and areas of a
country together. The same series come from the data of all areas with
`by = "country"` (this takes longer):

``` r

catch_shocks(load_fao_data(), by = "country", method = "gephart2017")
```

### Arguments and results

| Argument | Meaning | Default |
|----|----|----|
| `area_data` | FAO catch data: `fishing_area_data()$area_data`, or any subset of [`load_fao_data()`](https://linbojun99.github.io/faofishingreport/reference/load_fao_data.md) |  |
| `by` | What a series is: one or more of `"country"`, `"area"` and `"species"` | `c("country", "area")` |
| `method` | `"cottrell2019"` or `"gephart2017"` | `"cottrell2019"` |
| `min_years` | Series with catch in fewer years are left out | `20` |
| `top_n` | Number of series with the largest catch in the timeline chart | `25` |
| `plot`, `table`, `lang`, `pptx`, `label` | Common arguments (see the start of the page) |  |

| Element | Content |
|----|----|
| `shocks` | One row per shock: the series, `Year`, `catch_tonnes`, `baseline_tonnes`, `loss_tonnes`, `loss_pct`, `cooks_distance` and `recovery_years` |
| `by_year` | Each year: `n_series` (series with catch), `n_shocks` and `shock_frequency_pct` |
| `by_group` | Shock rate by `grouping` (country, area, species, continent, species group): `n_series`, `n_shocks` and `shocks_per_series` |
| `series` | The series analysed: `first_year`, `last_year`, `n_years`, `total_tonnes` and `n_shocks` |

- Both studies analysed national totals. Series of one country in one
  area, or of one species, use the same method on smaller units.
- Highly variable series (e.g. Peruvian anchoveta) may show no shocks,
  because large changes are usual in them (Gephart et al. 2017).
- A shock is an anomaly of the catch series. It may come from the stock,
  the environment, markets, management or a change in reporting; the
  catch data do not say which.
- The smoother and the regression use the whole series, so a new year of
  data can change which earlier years are found as shocks.

## 💥 Fishery collapses

Two definitions of a collapse from catch data are widely used. Mullon et
al. (2005) counted the collapses in FAO catch series and described the
shape of the decline before them; Worm et al. (2006) followed the share
of fisheries whose catch was below 10% of its maximum. Wilberg and
Miller (2007) showed that the second measure also rises for random
series with no trend, which is why
[`collapse_analysis()`](https://linbojun99.github.io/faofishingreport/reference/collapse_analysis.md)
compares the data with such random series.

### Method

|  | `"mullon2005"` (default) | `"worm2006"` |
|----|----|----|
| A series is | One species or genus caught by one country in one FAO area | One species item in one FAO area, all countries together |
| Left out | Items not identified to genus or species; the countries in `exclude_countries`; series with a missing year among the last `complete_years` (20) years; series with a mean catch below `min_mean_catch` (500 t a year) | Fisheries with a total catch below `min_total_catch` (10,000 t) |
| Collapsed | After the year of the maximum catch $`X_{max}`$, the catch stays below $`X_{max}/10`$ for 4 consecutive years; the first of them is the collapse year $`D_c`$ (Mullon et al. 2005, p. 113) | In each year when the catch is below 10% of the maximum; recovered when back above. A fishery starts when its catch first reaches 10% of the maximum |
| Results | Number of collapses, their years and the shape of the decline | Share of fisheries collapsed in each year, and share that have collapsed at least once (Worm et al. 2006, main text and supplementary pp. 4–5) |

By default `exclude_countries` holds the countries that Mullon et
al. (2005, p. 112) left out: the former USSR, Yugoslavia and
Czechoslovakia, whose series end with the country; South Africa and
Namibia, whose series were split; and China, whose series they
considered distorted.

**Shape of the decline** (Mullon et al. 2005, p. 114), checked in this
order (the paper does not give an order):

| Type | Rule |
|----|----|
| Plateau | Catch above $`X_{max}/4`$ in every year from $`D_c - 8`$ to $`D_c - 3`$: a sudden fall after a long period of high catch |
| Smooth | Correlation between catch and time from $`D_c - 10`$ to $`D_c`$ below $`-0.7`$: a long, regular decline |
| Erratic | Otherwise: a fall after several ups and downs |
| Not classified | Collapses less than 10 years after the first year of the series |

Mullon et al. found 366 collapses among 1,519 FAO series from 1950 to
2000 (24%): 21% plateau, 33% smooth and 45% erratic.

**Null model.** The maximum of a series grows with its length, so a
share of “collapsed” fisheries defined against the maximum rises over
time even when nothing changes (Wilberg and Miller 2007). With
`null_model = TRUE` (default) the analysis is repeated on `n_sim` (100)
sets of random series with no trend, with the same start years and
lengths as the real series. As in Wilberg and Miller (2007), they are
stationary first-order autoregressive lognormal series:
$`x_t = \rho\,x_{t-1} + \varepsilon_t`$ with $`\rho = 0.75`$ and
$`\varepsilon_t \sim N\!\left(0,\ \sigma^2 (1 - \rho^2)\right)`$, and
catch $`= e^{x_t}`$, where $`\sigma^2 = \ln(1 + \text{CV}^2)`$ for a
coefficient of variation of 80%. The share of collapses in these series
is the level that the definition gives by itself.

**Random numbers.** The random series are drawn again at every run, so
the results of the null model change slightly from one run to the next.
[`set.seed()`](https://rdrr.io/r/base/Random.html) before the call fixes
them. This page uses `set.seed(1)` so that the numbers in the text match
the tables at every build of the site;
[`fao_report()`](https://linbojun99.github.io/faofishingreport/reference/fao_report.md)
does the same with `collapse_seed` (default 1).

### Example

``` r

set.seed(1)   # fixes the random series of the null model
collapses <- collapse_analysis(FAO34$area_data)
```

![Atlantic\_\_Eastern_Central_collapse_mullon2005.png](data:image/png;base64,)

`figures/png/summary/Atlantic__Eastern_Central_collapse_mullon2005.png`

![Atlantic\_\_Eastern_Central_collapse_mullon2005_types.png](data:image/png;base64,)

`figures/png/summary/Atlantic__Eastern_Central_collapse_mullon2005_types.png`

![Atlantic\_\_Eastern_Central_collapse_mullon2005_by_group.png](data:image/png;base64,)

`figures/png/summary/Atlantic__Eastern_Central_collapse_mullon2005_by_group.png`

The first chart is the number of collapses in each year, by type of
decline. The second is the mean catch of each type relative to its
maximum, from 10 years before to 5 years after the collapse year; the
dashed lines are $`X_{max}/4`$ and $`X_{max}/10`$. The third is the
share of collapsed series in each ISSCAAP species group with at least 3
series.

``` r

s <- collapses$summary
show_table(data.frame(s, row.names = NULL), digits = 1)
```

| Shads                         |        4 |           0 |           0.0 |

**Reading the results.** In area 34, 73 of the 263 series (27.8%)
collapsed by the definition of Mullon et al. (2005), against 17.2% in
random series with no trend. The difference, not the share itself, is
what points to real collapses. Of the collapses, 38% were erratic, 23%
plateau and 19% smooth. Plateau collapses are the hardest to foresee:
the catch stays high until it falls (Mullon et al. 2005).

### Other settings

The definition of Worm et al. (2006), with the same seed:

``` r

set.seed(1)
worm <- collapse_analysis(FAO34$area_data, method = "worm2006")
```

![Atlantic\_\_Eastern_Central_collapse_worm2006.png](data:image/png;base64,)

`figures/png/summary/Atlantic__Eastern_Central_collapse_worm2006.png`

The solid lines are the data and the dashed lines the random series of
the null model: in red the share of fisheries that have collapsed at
least once, in blue the share collapsed in the year.

``` r

show_table(data.frame(worm$summary, row.names = NULL), digits = 1)
```

| type                       |   n | n_series | pct_of_series | null_pct_of_series |
|:---------------------------|----:|---------:|--------------:|-------------------:|
| collapsed in the last year |  28 |      178 |          15.7 |               12.9 |
| collapsed at least once    | 134 |      178 |          75.3 |               80.6 |

``` r

show_table(data.frame(subset(worm$by_year, Year %in% c(1960, 1980, 2000, max(Year))), row.names = NULL), digits = 1)
```

| Year | n_fisheries | n_collapsed | n_ever_collapsed | pct_current | pct_cumulative | null_pct_current | null_pct_cumulative |
|:---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 1960 | 29 | 1 | 5 | 3.4 | 17.2 | 13.8 | 36.3 |
| 1980 | 121 | 29 | 73 | 24.0 | 60.3 | 13.9 | 58.9 |
| 2000 | 155 | 40 | 114 | 25.8 | 73.5 | 12.9 | 73.9 |
| 2024 | 178 | 28 | 134 | 15.7 | 75.3 | 12.9 | 80.6 |

By the last year, 75.3% of the fisheries of area 34 had collapsed at
least once, but random series with no trend give 80.6%: in this area the
rising cumulative share comes from the definition, which is the point
made by Wilberg and Miller (2007). The share collapsed in the last year,
15.7% against 12.9% in the null model, is the better indicator.

Three more settings are often useful: `exclude_countries = character(0)`
keeps all countries with the method of Mullon et al.;
`null_model = FALSE` skips the random series, which is faster;
`n_sim = 1000` gives a steadier null model.

### Arguments and results

| Argument | Meaning | Default |
|----|----|----|
| `area_data` | FAO catch data: `fishing_area_data()$area_data`, or any subset of [`load_fao_data()`](https://linbojun99.github.io/faofishingreport/reference/load_fao_data.md) |  |
| `method` | `"mullon2005"` or `"worm2006"` | `"mullon2005"` |
| `exclude_countries` | Countries left out with `"mullon2005"` | `c("Un. Sov. Soc. Rep.", "Yugoslavia SFR", "Czechoslovakia", "South Africa", "Namibia", "China")` |
| `complete_years` | With `"mullon2005"`, series need a record in each of the last this many years of the data | `20` |
| `min_mean_catch` | With `"mullon2005"`, minimum mean catch of a series (t a year) | `500` |
| `min_total_catch` | With `"worm2006"`, minimum total catch of a fishery (t) | `10000` |
| `null_model` | Repeat the analysis on random series with no trend (Wilberg and Miller 2007) | `TRUE` |
| `n_sim` | Number of random data sets of the null model | `100` |
| `plot`, `table`, `lang`, `pptx`, `label` | Common arguments (see the start of the page) |  |

| Element | Content |
|----|----|
| `series` | One row per series: `max_year` and `max_tonnes`; with `"mullon2005"` also `collapsed`, `collapse_year` and `type`; with `"worm2006"` `start_year`, `collapsed_last_year` and `first_collapse_year` |
| `summary` | `"mullon2005"`: number of collapses and of each type, `pct_of_series`, `pct_of_collapses` and the share in the null model `null_pct_of_series`. `"worm2006"`: fisheries collapsed in the last year and at least once, with the null model |
| `by_year` | `"mullon2005"`: `n_collapses` by year and type. `"worm2006"`: `n_fisheries`, `n_collapsed`, `n_ever_collapsed`, `pct_current`, `pct_cumulative`, and the same shares in the null model |
| `by_group` | Share of collapsed series by FAO area and species group: `n_series`, `n_collapsed` and `pct_collapsed` |

- Catch data alone cannot tell a collapse of the stock from a fall in
  catch caused by management, markets or reporting.
- A definition based on the maximum gives “collapses” in random series
  too. Compare the data with the null model, which is a reference level
  and not a statistical test.
- Worm et al. (2006) used species in large marine ecosystems from Sea
  Around Us data; here a fishery is a species item in an FAO area, so
  the shares are not directly comparable.
- With the default `exclude_countries`, the catch of China is left out,
  as by Mullon et al. (2005).

## 🎼 Synchrony and the portfolio effect

When the catches of different species rise and fall at different times,
their total varies less than each of them. This is the portfolio effect,
named after the way a diverse investment portfolio reduces risk. Ong et
al. (2021) analysed 1,092 marine catch series and found that regions
with more synchronous catches had less stable total catches.
[`catch_synchrony()`](https://linbojun99.github.io/faofishingreport/reference/catch_synchrony.md)
measures how synchronously the catch series of the data fluctuate, and
how much their asynchrony stabilises the total catch.

### Method

The series are chosen as by Ong et al. (2021): the median catch is above
`min_median` (10 t a year) and more than `min_nonzero` (3/4) of the
years have catch. With `by = "species"`, only items identified to
species are used (Ong et al. left out miscellaneous and “nei” items).
Each series is **detrended** with a linear regression on year, as by Ong
et al., since common trends make series look synchronous (Lepš et
al. 2019); `detrend = "none"` keeps the trends.

With $`\sigma_i`$ the standard deviation of series $`i`$ (after
detrending), $`\sigma_T`$ that of the total catch, $`m_i`$ the mean
catch of series $`i`$ and $`m_T`$ the mean total catch:

| Measure | Formula | Column |
|----|----|----|
| Synchrony | $`\varphi = \sigma_T^2 / \left(\sum_i \sigma_i\right)^2`$, from 0 (the fluctuations fully compensate each other) to 1 (perfectly synchronous) (Loreau and de Mazancourt 2008, eq. 9) | `synchrony_phi` |
| CV of the total | $`\text{CV}_T = \sigma_T / m_T`$ | `cv_total` |
| Weighted mean CV | $`\sum_i \sigma_i / m_T`$: the CV of the total if all series were perfectly synchronous | `weighted_mean_cv` |
| Decomposition | $`\text{CV}_T = \sqrt{\varphi} \times \sum_i \sigma_i / m_T`$ (Thibaut and Connolly 2013, eqs. 2–4): the lower the synchrony, the more stable the total |  |
| Mean CV of the series | $`\overline{\text{CV}} = \frac{1}{n} \sum_i \sigma_i / m_i`$ | `mean_cv_series` |
| Portfolio effect | $`100 \times (\overline{\text{CV}} - \text{CV}_T) / \text{CV}_T`$: how much more variable the single series are than their total, in percent (Ong et al. 2021, after Carlson and Satterthwaite 2011) | `portfolio_effect_pct` |
| Pairwise correlations | Correlations between the detrended series: their mean and the share that are positive | `mean_pairwise_correlation`, `positive_correlations_pct` |

The same measures are computed in moving windows of `window` years (20),
with the linear trend removed in each window (a choice of this package),
to show how synchrony changed over time. Ong et al. (2021) measured
synchrony with wavelet coherence, which separates time scales; this
function uses the simpler correlation-based measures above.

### Example

``` r

sync <- catch_synchrony(FAO34$area_data)
```

![Atlantic\_\_Eastern_Central_synchrony_species.png](data:image/png;base64,)

`figures/png/summary/Atlantic__Eastern_Central_synchrony_species.png`

![Atlantic\_\_Eastern_Central_synchrony_species_cv.png](data:image/png;base64,)

`figures/png/summary/Atlantic__Eastern_Central_synchrony_species_cv.png`

![Atlantic\_\_Eastern_Central_synchrony_species_correlation.png](data:image/png;base64,)

`figures/png/summary/Atlantic__Eastern_Central_synchrony_species_correlation.png`

The first chart is the synchrony and the portfolio effect in each
20-year window, plotted at the middle year of the window. The second
compares the CV of the total catch (red, dashed line) with the CV of the
`top_n` largest series. The third shows the correlations between these
series: red for series that rise and fall together, blue for series that
compensate each other.

``` r

show_table(sync$summary[, c("n_series", "synchrony_phi", "cv_total", "weighted_mean_cv", "mean_cv_series",
                            "portfolio_effect_pct", "mean_pairwise_correlation")], digits = 2)
```

| n_series | synchrony_phi | cv_total | weighted_mean_cv | mean_cv_series | portfolio_effect_pct | mean_pairwise_correlation |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 52 | 0.2 | 0.18 | 0.41 | 0.76 | 314.25 | 0.05 |

``` r

with(sync$summary, c(cv_total = cv_total, decomposition = sqrt(synchrony_phi) * weighted_mean_cv))
#>      cv_total decomposition 
#>     0.1837505     0.1837505
```

The second line checks the decomposition of Thibaut and Connolly (2013):
the CV of the total is $`\sqrt{\varphi}`$ times the weighted mean CV.
For each series, `share_of_variability_pct` is its share of
$`\sum_i \sigma_i`$:

``` r

show_table(sync$series[, c("series", "mean_tonnes", "sd_tonnes", "cv", "share_of_variability_pct")], digits = 2)
```

| series | mean_tonnes | sd_tonnes | cv | share_of_variability_pct |
|:---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| European pilchard(=Sardine) | 595,902.46 | 178,774.58 | 0.30 | 25.08 |
| Round sardinella | 185,901.85 | 101,080.57 | 0.54 | 14.18 |
| Atlantic chub mackerel | 177,641.72 | 63,622.56 | 0.36 | 8.93 |
| Bonga shad | 148,363.16 | 34,805.99 | 0.23 | 4.88 |
| Skipjack tuna | 100,172.93 | 24,511.51 | 0.24 | 3.44 |
| European anchovy | 87,213.08 | 58,444.49 | 0.67 | 8.20 |
| Yellowfin tuna | 81,282.49 | 29,532.82 | 0.36 | 4.14 |
| Madeiran sardinella | 79,641.14 | 36,174.91 | 0.45 | 5.07 |
| Bigeye tuna | 36,937.61 | 17,403.33 | 0.47 | 2.44 |

``` r

show_table(data.frame(subset(sync$windows, first_year %% 10 == 0), row.names = NULL), digits = 2)
```

| first_year | last_year | mid_year | n_series | synchrony_phi | cv_total | mean_cv_series | portfolio_effect_pct |
|:---|:---|:---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 1950 | 1969 | 1959.5 | 52 | 0.24 | 0.20 | 0.98 | 384.42 |
| 1960 | 1979 | 1969.5 | 52 | 0.26 | 0.21 | 0.66 | 214.74 |
| 1970 | 1989 | 1979.5 | 52 | 0.31 | 0.17 | 0.47 | 170.92 |
| 1980 | 1999 | 1989.5 | 52 | 0.36 | 0.18 | 0.43 | 144.52 |
| 1990 | 2009 | 1999.5 | 52 | 0.27 | 0.11 | 0.44 | 299.22 |
| 2000 | 2019 | 2009.5 | 52 | 0.18 | 0.07 | 0.44 | 509.90 |

**Reading the results.** The 52 species series of area 34 have a
synchrony of 0.20, far from 1: their fluctuations largely compensate
each other. The CV of the total catch, 0.18, is 0.44
($`\sqrt{\varphi}`$) times what it would be if all species fluctuated
together (0.41). A single species series varies on average 4.1 times as
much as the total, a portfolio effect of 314%. The mean correlation
between two series is 0.05. In the moving windows, the synchrony was
0.24 in 1950–1969, reached 0.36 in 1980–1999 and fell to 0.13 in
2005–2024.

| by | detrend | n_series | synchrony_phi | cv_total | mean_cv_series | portfolio_effect_pct | mean_pairwise_correlation |
|:---|:---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| species | linear | 52 | 0.20 | 0.18 | 0.76 | 314.25 | 0.05 |
| species | none | 52 | 0.62 | 0.56 | 0.96 | 71.49 | 0.22 |
| country | linear | 29 | 0.10 | 0.13 | 0.58 | 345.47 | 0.04 |

Without detrending, the synchrony is 0.62 instead of 0.20: the catches
of most species grew over the decades, and this common trend makes the
series look synchronous (Lepš et al. 2019). The catches of the 29

### Arguments and results

| Argument | Meaning | Default |
|----|----|----|
| `area_data` | FAO catch data: `fishing_area_data()$area_data`, or any subset of [`load_fao_data()`](https://linbojun99.github.io/faofishingreport/reference/load_fao_data.md) |  |
| `by` | What a series is: `"species"` or `"country"` | `"species"` |
| `detrend` | `"linear"` to remove a linear trend from each series, or `"none"` | `"linear"` |
| `window` | Length of the moving windows (years) | `20` |
| `top_n` | Number of series with the largest catch in the CV and correlation charts | `20` |
| `min_median` | Series need a median catch above this many tonnes a year | `10` |
| `min_nonzero` | Series need catch in more than this share of the years | `0.75` |
| `plot`, `table`, `lang`, `pptx`, `label` | Common arguments (see the start of the page) |  |

| Element | Content |
|----|----|
| `summary` | `n_series`, `first_year`, `last_year`, `detrend`, `synchrony_phi`, `cv_total`, `weighted_mean_cv`, `mean_cv_series`, `portfolio_effect_pct`, `mean_pairwise_correlation` and `positive_correlations_pct` |
| `series` | Each series: `mean_tonnes`, `sd_tonnes` (after detrending), `cv` and `share_of_variability_pct` |
| `windows` | The measures in each moving window: `first_year`, `last_year`, `mid_year`, `n_series`, `synchrony_phi`, `cv_total`, `mean_cv_series` and `portfolio_effect_pct` (`NULL` when the data have fewer than `window` + 2 years) |
| `correlation` | Matrix of the pairwise correlations of the detrended series |

- Trends make series look synchronous (Lepš et al. 2019): compare
  `detrend = "linear"` and `"none"` before reading much into the
  synchrony.
- The measures are correlation-based. Ong et al. (2021) used wavelet
  coherence, which separates time scales and allows for lags.
- Catches can fluctuate together because of the fish or because of
  fishing: Ong et al. (2021) found that coherent catches can come from
  coherent biomass or from coherent fishing mortality.
- The mean CV of the series is not weighted, so small and variable
  series raise the portfolio effect; $`\varphi`$ and the weighted mean
  CV weight each series by its size.

## 🚢 Distant-water profile of a country

Since 1950 marine fisheries have spread over a growing part of the ocean
(Swartz et al. 2010).
[`distant_water_profile()`](https://linbojun99.github.io/faofishingreport/reference/distant_water_profile.md)
follows this expansion for one country with FAO statistics: its catch in
the FAO areas it borders and in those it does not border, the number of
areas in which it fishes each year, and the first and last year, peak
and recent catch in each area.

### Method

- **Distant-water catch** is defined as by FAO: the catch of a country
  in the FAO major fishing areas it does not border. Fishing outside its
  own waters but in an area it borders does not count (Grainger and
  Garcia 1996, section 2.6; Garibaldi and Limongelli 2003, section 2.1).
- An area is **adjacent** to a country when the country’s land,
  including overseas territories, lies within 20 km of the FAO area
  boundary. This is a rule of this package, the same as in
  [`coastal_distant()`](https://linbojun99.github.io/faofishingreport/reference/coastal_distant.md)
  (see [🔍 Data quality, diversity and
  fleets](https://linbojun99.github.io/faofishingreport/articles/quality-diversity-fleets.md)).
- An area counts as **fished** in a year when the country’s catch there
  is above `min_catch` tonnes (default 0, any reported catch).
- Inland fishing areas are left out.

FAO records the catch by the flag of the vessel and by FAO major area,
not by exclusive economic zone (EEZ). The profile shows in which FAO
areas a country’s fleet fished, not whether the catch came from its own
waters, the waters of other countries or the high seas. Swartz et
al. (2010) mapped the expansion with Sea Around Us catch maps; this
function uses FAO statistics only, at the resolution of FAO major areas.

### Example

The function takes a country, as named in the FAO data, and uses the
catch of all areas:

``` r

china <- distant_water_profile("China")
```

`share_of_distant_pct` is the share of each distant-water area in all
the distant-water catch of the country over the whole period. China
borders only the Northwest Pacific (area 61). It reported its first
catch in area 34 in 1986, and area 34 makes up 4.1% of its distant-water
catch.

For China, FAO notes that in 2022 China reported 2.3 million tonnes of
distant-water catch but gave species and areas only for the catch landed
in China (area 61). FAO filled the other areas with data from regional
fisheries management organizations and entered 1.3 million tonnes as
“Marine fishes nei” in area 61 (FAO 2024). The recent distant-water
catch of China is therefore partly counted in its adjacent area 61.

34, over the whole period (`share_of_distant_pct`) and over the last
five years (`recent_share_pct`), with the distant-water share of their
marine catch in the last year (`distant_pct_latest`):

``` r

others <- c("Russian Federation", "Netherlands (Kingdom of the)", "Japan", "Korea, Republic of")
profiles <- c(list(China = china, Spain = spain),
              sapply(others, distant_water_profile, plot = FALSE, table = FALSE, simplify = FALSE))
area34 <- do.call(rbind, lapply(names(profiles), function(country) {
  areas <- profiles[[country]]$areas
  here <- areas$area_en == "Atlantic, Eastern Central"
  recent <- 100 * areas$last_5_years_tonnes / sum(areas$last_5_years_tonnes[!areas$adjacent])
  data.frame(country = fao_translate(country, "country", lang = NULL),
             distant_pct_latest = tail(profiles[[country]]$yearly$distant_pct, 1),
             area34_adjacent = areas$adjacent[here],
             area34_first_year = areas$first_year[here],
             share_of_distant_pct = areas$share_of_distant_pct[here],
             recent_share_pct = ifelse(areas$adjacent[here], NA, recent[here]))
}))
show_table(area34, digits = 1)
```

| country | distant_pct_latest | area34_adjacent | area34_first_year | share_of_distant_pct | recent_share_pct |
|:---|---:|:---|:---|---:|---:|
| China | 6.1 | FALSE | 1986 | 4.1 | 0.5 |
| Spain | 54.2 | TRUE | 1950 | NA | NA |
| Russian Federation | 2.9 | FALSE | 1992 | 68.0 | 70.9 |
| Netherlands (Kingdom of the) | 7.2 | FALSE | 1996 | 83.7 | 100.0 |
| Japan | 7.6 | FALSE | 1950 | 5.1 | 6.7 |
| Korea, Republic of | 34.9 | FALSE | 1964 | 7.7 | 0.3 |

### Arguments and results

| Argument | Meaning | Default |
|----|----|----|
| `country_name` | The country, as named in the FAO data (e.g. `"China"`, `"Spain"`) |  |
| `top_n` | Number of distant-water areas shown separately; the others are combined | `8` |
| `min_catch` | An area counts as fished in a year when the country’s catch there is above this many tonnes | `0` |
| `data_version` | The FAO data release to use; see [`load_fao_data()`](https://linbojun99.github.io/faofishingreport/reference/load_fao_data.md) | `"latest"` |
| `plot`, `table`, `lang`, `pptx`, `label` | Common arguments (see the start of the page); `label` defaults to the country |  |

| Element | Content |
|----|----|
| `yearly` | Each year: `adjacent_tonnes`, `distant_tonnes`, `distant_pct`, `n_adjacent_areas`, `n_distant_areas` and `n_areas` (areas fished) |
| `areas` | One row per FAO area fished: `adjacent`, `first_year` and `last_year` with catch above `min_catch`, `n_years`, `peak_year`, `peak_tonnes`, `last_5_years_tonnes`, `total_tonnes` and `share_of_distant_pct` (empty for adjacent areas) |
| `distant` | Yearly catch in each distant-water area (`top_n` areas, the others combined) |

## 🔁 Revisions between FAO releases

FAO publishes a new release of the Global Capture Production data every
year. A release adds the latest year and also revises earlier years when
countries send corrected or more complete data (Garibaldi 2012). Zeller
and Pauly (2018) call “presentist bias” the practice of applying
improvements in reporting to recent years only, without revising the
earlier years, which makes a time series show an increase that did not
happen.
[`compare_releases()`](https://linbojun99.github.io/faofishingreport/reference/compare_releases.md)
compares two releases record by record and shows which years and
countries were revised, and how far back the revisions reach.

### Method

A record is the catch of one country, species item and FAO area in one
year. Each record of the two releases is put in one class:

| Class | Rule |
|----|----|
| `revised` | In both releases, with catches that differ by more than `tolerance` (0.5 t, rounding) |
| `added` | Only in the new release, for a year the older release already covered |
| `removed` | Only in the older release |
| `reclassified` | Removed under one species item and added under another with the same country, area, year and catch, e.g. when FAO renames or splits a species item; not counted as a revision |
| `new year` | In a year after the last year of the older release |
| `unchanged` | Everything else |

The function then sums the catch of each year in both releases and the
revisions by country, and counts the records whose status flag changed
(e.g. from an estimate to an official figure). The releases are compared
on the names used by the package, matched through the FAO codes when a
release is downloaded. No published study has compared successive
FishStat releases record by record in this way: the comparison is a tool
of this package, and the two papers above give the background.

### Example

The comparison needs both releases on the computer. The newest release
is bundled with the package; download older ones with
[`download_fao_data()`](https://linbojun99.github.io/faofishingreport/reference/download_fao_data.md)
(about 5 MB each, from FAO).
[`check_fao_update()`](https://linbojun99.github.io/faofishingreport/reference/check_fao_update.md)
lists the releases available.

``` r

check_fao_update()               # releases available from FAO
download_fao_data("2025.1.0")    # download an older release
```

``` r

releases <- compare_releases("2025.1.0", "2026.1.0", area_name = "Atlantic, Eastern Central")
```

![Atlantic\_\_Eastern_Central_releases_2025_1_0_vs_2026_1_0.png](data:image/png;base64,)

`figures/png/summary/Atlantic__Eastern_Central_releases_2025_1_0_vs_2026_1_0.png`

![Atlantic\_\_Eastern_Central_releases_2025_1_0_vs_2026_1_0_by_year.png](data:image/png;base64,)

`figures/png/summary/Atlantic__Eastern_Central_releases_2025_1_0_vs_2026_1_0_by_year.png`

![Atlantic\_\_Eastern_Central_releases_2025_1_0_vs_2026_1_0_countries.png](data:image/png;base64,)

`figures/png/summary/Atlantic__Eastern_Central_releases_2025_1_0_vs_2026_1_0_countries.png`

The first chart is the total catch of each year in the two releases. The
second is the revision of each year’s total (new minus old release), in
thousand tonnes. The third gives the net revision of the `top_n`
countries with the largest revisions, ranked by the sum of their
absolute revisions: a country can rank high with a small net revision
when its revisions up and down cancel out.

``` r

table(releases$records$change)
#> 
#>        added reclassified      removed      revised 
#>          159         1132           47          664
show_table(data.frame(tail(releases$by_year, 10), row.names = NULL), digits = 1)
```

`records` keeps only the records that changed. The largest revisions:

``` r

records <- releases$records[order(-abs(releases$records$difference)), ]
show_table(data.frame(records[, c("country_name", "species_name", "Year", "tonnes_old", "tonnes_new",
                                  "difference", "change", "status_old", "status_new")], row.names = NULL),
           digits = 0)
```

| country_name | species_name | Year | tonnes_old | tonnes_new | difference | change | status_old | status_new |
|:---|:---|:---|---:|---:|---:|:---|:---|:---|
| Mauritania | European pilchard(=Sardine) | 2023 | 301,105 | 210,000 | -91,105 | revised | estimate | estimate |
| Mauritania | Madeiran sardinella | 2023 | 166,820 | 120,000 | -46,820 | revised | estimate | estimate |
| Mauritania | European pilchard(=Sardine) | 2022 | 295,205 | 250,000 | -45,205 | revised | estimate | estimate |
| Mauritania | Madeiran sardinella | 2022 | 163,551 | 125,000 | -38,551 | revised | estimate | estimate |
| Mauritania | Marine fishes nei | 2020 | 18,255 | 2,423 | -15,832 | revised | estimate | estimate |
| Morocco | Marine fishes nei | 2021 | 12,127 | 26,696 | 14,569 | revised | estimate | actual |
| Mauritania | Atlantic bonito | 2022 | NA | 10,843 | 10,843 | added | NA | actual |
| Morocco | Marine fishes nei | 2017 | 42,843 | 32,740 | -10,103 | revised | estimate | actual |
| Guatemala | Skipjack tuna | 2017 | 9,886 | 0 | -9,886 | revised | actual | actual |
| Mauritania | Marine fishes nei | 2021 | 19,840 | 11,026 | -8,814 | revised | actual | estimate |

**Reading the results.** Between the two releases, 664 records of area
34 were revised, 159 added and 47 removed. Most of them concern the last
ten years covered by the older release (655 of the revised records), and
the largest revisions are in the last two years. The total catch of 2023
went down by 136 thousand tonnes (2.6%). The 1,132 reclassified records
are catches moved from one species item to another, which leave the
totals unchanged.

### Other settings

One country, ignoring changes of 100 t or less:

``` r

mauritania <- compare_releases("2025.1.0", "2026.1.0", area_name = "Atlantic, Eastern Central",
                               country_name = "Mauritania", tolerance = 100)
```

|:---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|

| 2018 | 952,706.8 | 952,706.8 | 0.0 | 0.0 | 2 | 4 | 0 | 1 |

For Mauritania, the revisions up to 2021 moved catch between species
items and left the yearly totals unchanged; the revisions of the last
two years lowered the totals by 10.0% and 16.9%. Without `area_name` and
`country_name` the whole data set is compared; without `old` and `new`
the newest release on the computer is compared with the one before it.

### Arguments and results

| Argument | Meaning | Default |
|----|----|----|
| `old`, `new` | The releases to compare, e.g. `"2025.1.0"` and `"2026.1.0"`, or `"bundled"` for the data bundled with the package | `NULL`: the newest release on the computer for `new`, and the one before it for `old` |
| `area_name` | FAO fishing areas to compare | `NULL` (all) |
| `country_name` | Countries to compare | `NULL` (all) |
| `tolerance` | Changes of at most this many tonnes are ignored | `0.5` |
| `top_n` | Number of countries with the largest revisions in the country chart | `10` |
| `data_dir` | Folder where the downloaded releases are stored | [`fao_data_dir()`](https://linbojun99.github.io/faofishingreport/reference/fao_data_dir.md) |
| `plot`, `table`, `lang`, `pptx`, `label` | Common arguments (see the start of the page); `label` defaults to the areas and countries compared |  |

| Element | Content |
|----|----|
| `by_year` | Each year covered by the older release: `old_tonnes`, `new_tonnes`, `change_tonnes`, `change_pct`, and the numbers of records `n_revised`, `n_added`, `n_removed`, `n_reclassified` and `n_status_changed` |
| `by_country` | Revisions by country, without reclassified records: `net_change_tonnes`, `abs_change_tonnes`, `n_records`, `first_year` and `last_year` |
| `records` | Every revised, added, removed or reclassified record: `tonnes_old`, `tonnes_new`, `status_old`, `status_new`, `difference`, `change` and `status_changed` |
| `releases` | The two releases compared |

- Recent years are revised most, because their figures are often
  provisional or estimated when first published (see
  [`data_quality()`](https://linbojun99.github.io/faofishingreport/reference/data_quality.md)
  in [🔍 Data quality, diversity and
  fleets](https://linbojun99.github.io/faofishingreport/articles/quality-diversity-fleets.md)).
- A record counts as reclassified only when the same catch moves to
  another species item. When FAO splits one item into several with
  different catches, the change shows as records removed and added.
- Revisions show what FAO changed, not which release is right.
